b2-w7-new-q15-15.stem: Which are essential components of a preventative health visit for older adults?
b2-w7-new-q15-15.lead: The correct answer is E. The periodic health encounter for older adults runs on ALBUS: Acute issues and safety, Labs and vitals, Book follow-up, Update profile, Screening. options: The hormone vasopressin reduces thirst.
Prolonged hyperosmolarity can lead to fatal brain swelling.
Less aldosterone will be secreted by the adrenal cortex.
There will be a dramatically increased secretion of renin from the kidneys.
b2-w5-meds2024-q5-5.answer:
The correct answer is C.

Aldosterone signals the kidneys to reabsorb water indirectly, by directly reabsorbing sodium. With the blood already hyperosmolar, the kidneys reabsorb less sodium to keep it from rising further. Hyperosmolar blood draws water out of brain cells, so they shrink rather than swell (B).
b2-w5-meds2024-q5-5.why: The source printed the brain-swelling option twice (B and C). The duplicate is removed, which moves the aldosterone answer from D to C; the answer itself is unchanged. Reader report #329.

option.E: Of the two autonomic divisions, only the sympathetic nervous system innervates blood vessels: vessel diameter is changed by raising or lowering tonic sympathetic firing.

b2-w5-meds2024-q8-8.why: E said constriction and dilation are controlled exclusively by the sympathetic system, which overlooks local and hormonal control. The lecture's point is narrower (02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation: the parasympathetic system does not innervate blood vessels; tone is set by tonic sympathetic firing), and E now says that. Key unchanged. Reader report #313.

option.C: Epinephrine can both dilate and constrict blood vessels, depending on which adrenergic receptor (alpha or beta-2) predominates in that vascular bed.

b2-w5-meds2024-q9-9.why: C now names the receptor type, alpha or beta-2, as the explanation does; the vascular bed only decides which receptor predominates. Key unchanged. Reader report #315.

  1. Endocrine signaling involves secreting hormones into the bloodstream and therefore is a slower signaling pathway than other direct methods.

  3. Half of lymph returns to the cardiovascular system through the right lymphatic duct.

b2-w6-meds2024-q6-6.answer:
The correct answer is D.

A known BRCA-1 carrier is high risk, so she is screened through the High Risk Ontario Breast Screening Program: an annual breast MRI together with a mammogram, ages 30 to 69. Mammography alone (A) is the average-risk screen. CT and PET are not screening tests, and choosing wisely argues against them.
b2-w6-meds2024-q6-6.why: The source keyed MRI alone, but the lecture screens high-risk women with MRI as an adjunct to mammography, annually from 30 to 69 (03 - Cancer Genetics; 07 - Well Person Care and Screening for Cancer). D now says both. The explanation also carried a stray line about dysplasia from another question, now removed. Reader report #321.

b2-w6-meds2024-q10-10.answer:
The correct answer is C.

If a cell receives damage to the same gene on both chromosomes this can produce cancer. The first hit can be inherited and the second hit can be acquired through life.
b2-w6-meds2024-q10-10.why: The explanation carried a line about FIT and colonoscopy from another question; it is removed. Key unchanged. Reader report #323.

option.C: A deleterious mutation to one copy of BRCA-1 or BRCA-2 in someone with two normal copies still leaves a functional copy. Heterozygous carriers do not have this advantage.

b2-w6-meds2024-q21-21.answer:
The correct answer is C.

This question refers to the two-hit hypothesis. Someone born with two normal copies has a buffer: one damaged copy still leaves a working one. A carrier of a BRCA-1 or BRCA-2 mutation has only one functional copy, so if that copy is damaged, cancer may result (assuming other genes mutate as well).
b2-w6-meds2024-q21-21.why: C said 'in homozygotes', meaning people with two normal copies, which read as if they carried two mutations. C and the explanation now say it plainly. Key unchanged. Reader report #331.

b2-w8-meds2024-q25-25.answer:
The correct answer is E.

Phase IV is post-marketing surveillance: once Health Canada approves a drug, it keeps being watched for safety in the wider population (09 - Canada's Healthcare System). E describes it as a study of cost-effectiveness and health-system use, which is not what Phase IV is. A to D match the lecture: animal efficacy and toxicity before any human trial, first trials in humans (about 20 to 80 people), first trials in select patients (about 100 to 300), then head-to-head against the standard of care.
b2-w8-meds2024-q25-25.why: The explanation only repeated option E word for word, so it never said what was wrong with it. Rewritten from the lecture; key unchanged. Reader reports #294, #296.

b2-w5-new-q22-22.lead: The correct answer is E. Working tissues - the gut, skeletal muscle and the heart - add CO2 to the blood; the lungs take it out.
b2-w5-new-q22-22.why: 03 - Body Systems Integration: capillaries in the tissues remove CO2 from them into the blood, and respiration moves CO2 from the red cells to the bronchial tree, so the lungs are where CO2 leaves the blood, not where it is added.

b2-w8-meds2024-q6-6.lead: The correct answers are C and D. C: Drug C reaches the full response, so it is not a partial agonist. D: a non-competitive antagonist lowers the maximal response but does not change potency, so it could not turn Drug B into Drug A, which is more potent than B.
b2-w8-meds2024-q6-6.why: 05 - Principles of Clinical Pharmacology: non-competitive antagonists reduce the efficacy of an agonist but do not change its potency. Drug A's half-maximal concentration sits well left of Drug B's, so D is false as well as C.

b2-w8-meds2024-q7-7.lead: The correct answer is C. Reducing a drug's potency raises its EC50 - more drug is needed for half the maximal effect - so BK-562 could not decrease heroin's EC50.
b2-w8-meds2024-q7-7.why: 03 - Pharmacodynamics: potency is the concentration giving 50% of the maximal effect (EC50), and a less potent drug needs more of it, so lower potency means a higher EC50. The key stands; the explanation now says EC50, as the option does.

option.G: Patients with severe von Willebrand's disease (vWD)

b3-w10-meds2024-q31-31.answer:
The correct answer is B, D, E, G, H.

The aPTT runs through the intrinsic pathway (factors XII, XI, IX and VIII) and then the common pathway (X, V, II and fibrinogen). Hemophilia A is a lack of factor VIII; the lupus anticoagulant is an antibody against the phospholipid the test depends on; severe vWD lowers von Willebrand factor, the chaperone that keeps factor VIII in circulation. In afibrinogenemia there is no fibrinogen for the clot the test times, so the aPTT (and the PT) are prolonged.

C and D turn on the mixing study, not on the factor. A 50:50 mix with normal plasma corrects a factor deficiency, so the aPTT of the mix in C is normal; it does not correct an inhibitor, so the aPTT of the mix in D stays elevated.
b3-w10-meds2024-q31-31.why: Reader report #101: afibrinogenemia also prolongs the aPTT. 02 - Hemostasis lists severe factor I deficiency among the causes of a raised PT/INR and aPTT, since fibrinogen is in the common pathway both tests end in; only mild to moderate deficiency leaves them normal. H is now keyed, and the stem asks for all that apply instead of four. Reader report #61 asked about C: the mix in C corrects, so its aPTT is normal, and the key still leaves it out. Option G's garbled text is repaired.

b3-w9-meds2024-q25-25.answer:
The correct answer is A.

Agglutination is antibody-mediated clumping. In cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia, IgM binds red cells below body temperature and, being a pentamer, bridges many cells together, which is why it is also called cold agglutinin disease.

In sickle cell disease, deoxygenated HbS polymerizes inside each cell and deforms it into a sickle. The cells block small vessels, but they do not agglutinate. In chronic inflammation, raised plasma proteins stack red cells into rouleaux, which is not agglutination either.
b3-w9-meds2024-q25-25.why: The bank keyed i and iii, but its own explanation describes sickling, not agglutination. 01 - Hematopoiesis gives one cause of agglutination, cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia (IgM bridges many RBCs together), and gives severe inflammation rouleaux instead. Reader report #93.

b3-wb-heme-q32.stem: A patient presents to your clinic with acute thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. Upon further examination you see schistocytes on the patient’s blood film, and lab findings report reduced ADAMTS-13 level. Which of the following disorders and treatments should the physician be considering?
options: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / Plasma exchange
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / Platelet exchange
Hemolytic uremic syndrome / Supportive therapy (IV fluids)
Hemolytic uremic syndrome / Hemodialysis
Disseminated intravascular coagulation / Supportive therapy (IV fluids)
b3-wb-heme-q32.answer:
The correct answer is A.

Thrombocytopenia, schistocytes (a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia) and kidney injury with a low ADAMTS-13 level is TTP. TTP is treated with plasma exchange, with corticosteroids and rituximab. Platelets are avoided: transfused platelets feed further thrombosis in TTP and HUS. HUS shares the picture but has a normal ADAMTS-13, and DIC prolongs the clotting times rather than lowering ADAMTS-13.
b3-wb-heme-q32.why: The extractor ran options C, D and E together into one line, so only three options showed. They are split back out, and ADAMSTS-13 is corrected to ADAMTS-13. Reader reports #99 and #108.

b3-w12-new-q13-13.answer:
The correct answer is E.

Both B and D are false. B: the abnormal protein upsets the osteoclast/osteoblast balance in favour of osteoclasts, so bone is resorbed and calcium rises. It is increased osteoclast activity, not osteoblast. D: myeloma is a clonal cancer of plasma cells, which are mature B lymphocytes, not T helper cells.

A and C are true: crowding of the marrow and local inflammation cause the anemia, and excess M protein can injure the kidney.
b3-w12-new-q13-13.why: Reader report #104 read the explanation as contradicting option D. It was naming the correction: D is false because myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells, which are B lymphocytes (06 - Multiple Myeloma). The explanation now says which option each sentence answers.

b3-wb-heme-q105.stem: Based on the abnormality of the white blood cells seen in the blood film shown on the right, what is the most likely diagnosis?
b3-wb-heme-q105.why: The film shows two neutrophils with pseudo-Pelger-Huet nuclei, a white cell finding, and the red cells around them are normal; the stem said red blood cells. Reader report #106.

b3-wb-heme-q4.answer:
The correct answer is B.

Hemoglobin H is a tetramer of four beta chains. It forms when alpha chains are too scarce to pair with them, so it is found in alpha-thalassemia (HbH disease, three alpha genes deleted) and not in beta-thalassemia. It shows on electrophoresis and on an HbH inclusion test.

Beta-thalassemia instead raises HbA2 and often HbF, so the absence of HbF does not separate the two. Both are microcytic. Ring sideroblasts, iron-laden mitochondria ringing the nucleus of red cell precursors, belong to sideroblastic anemia.
b3-wb-heme-q4.why: Reader report #114 is right about the explanation, which had alpha and beta reversed; the key stands. 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia: three deleted alpha genes give HbH disease, the HbH inclusion test is an alpha-thalassemia test, and beta-thalassemia raises HbA2. So finding HbH still points to alpha-thalassemia, and B is the answer.

b3-w9-meds2024-q15-15.answer:
The correct answer is B.

Hypersegmented neutrophils in a macrocytic anemia mean a megaloblastic anemia, from B12 or folate deficiency. Only B12 deficiency causes neurologic signs (loss of proprioception, neuropathy, cognitive change), so the normal neurological and mental status exam is what points this question to folate. Liver disease gives round macrocytes with normal neutrophils, and the rare drinking makes it less likely still.

That is a question-writing shortcut rather than a rule. Early B12 deficiency can have no neurologic signs yet, so in practice both B12 and folate are measured, and folic acid is never given alone until B12 deficiency is excluded: it corrects the anemia but not the nerve damage.
b3-w9-meds2024-q15-15.why: Reader report #117 argued for B12. The key stands: 05 - Approach to Macrocytic Anemia says only B12 deficiency gives neurologic signs, so a normal exam is the clue the question gives for folate. The reader's point is fair, though, since early B12 deficiency can lack those signs; the explanation now says so, and that both levels are checked before treating.

b3-w11-meds2024-q39-39.stem: Key feature question: A patient with a neutrophil count of 0.2 E9/L presents at the emergency department with a fever of 39 °C. Which treatments are appropriate? Select all that apply.
b3-w11-meds2024-q39-39.answer:
The correct answer is A, C.

Febrile neutropenia is an oncologic emergency, and the patient starts empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics at once: a carbapenem such as imipenem, or piperacillin-tazobactam. Vancomycin is added only for a line or skin infection or hemodynamic instability. Leukocyte transfusion is not used, imatinib treats CML, B12 treats a deficiency, and hydroxyurea lowers counts that are too high.
b3-w11-meds2024-q39-39.why: The source asks for the best three treatments but keys two, and no third option is right: 03 - Approach to Leukopenia treats febrile neutropenia with empiric IV imipenem or IV piperacillin-tazobactam, adding vancomycin only for a line or skin infection or instability. The stem now asks for all that apply, so the page no longer says select 2 under a stem that says three. Reader reports #121 and #128.

b3-w11-new-q10-10.stem:
Place the following actions in order for the management of febrile neutropenia:

  1. History and physical (head and neck, skin and indwelling catheters, mental status, etc.)
  2. Order investigations (CBC, blood culture, etc.)
  3. Stabilize patient
  4. Administer antibiotics empirically
options: i, ii, iii, iv
iii, i, ii, iv
iii, ii, i, iv
iii, iv, ii, i
b3-w11-new-q10-10.answer:
The correct answer is C (iii, ii, i, iv).

From 03 - Approach to Leukopenia. The lecture numbers the febrile neutropenia protocol in this order:

  • 1. iii stabilize - ABCs, IV fluids, and O2 for hypoxia.
  • 2. ii investigate - CBC and differential, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, transaminases and bilirubin, blood and urine cultures, and a CXR.
  • 3. i focused history and exam - mouth, pharynx and sinuses, lungs, GI (no DRE), GU, skin and catheter sites, and mental status.
  • 4. iv empiric antibiotics - IV imipenem or piperacillin-tazobactam, adding vancomycin for a line or skin infection or instability.

Cultures come before antibiotics so the organism can still be grown, but the antibiotics must not be delayed: this is an oncologic emergency.
b3-w11-new-q10-10.why: The bank asks for an order, but the page takes a set of picks, so there was no way to enter one. The four actions are now numbered in the stem and the options are orders to choose from. The sequence is the one the bank gave (stabilize, investigate, history and exam, antibiotics). Reader report #123.

b3-wb-heme-q23.stem: Which of the following disease states increase measured hematocrit? Select all that apply.
b3-wb-heme-q23.answer:
The correct answer is A, D.

Hypoxia from COPD raises erythropoietin, which drives a secondary erythrocytosis: the red cell mass and the measured hematocrit both rise. In apparent (relative) polycythemia the red cell mass is normal, but a contracted plasma volume from dehydration or diuretics concentrates the red cells, so the measured hematocrit is raised too. Aplastic anemia lowers it, and chronic myeloid leukemia usually leaves the red cells normal or reduced.
b3-wb-heme-q23.why: Reader report #140 is right. Apparent (relative) polycythemia is a raised hematocrit from a reduced plasma volume with a normal red cell mass, so the measured hematocrit is high by definition; it is the red cell mass that does not rise. 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis lists COPD as a hypoxic, secondary cause. A is keyed alongside D, and option A no longer calls it polycythemia vera, which is a different, primary disease.

b3-w9-meds2024-q8-8.answer:
The correct answer is A, C, G.

A low reticulocyte count with all three lines down (pancytopenia) points to the marrow. Aplastic anemia is a hypocellular, fatty marrow that makes too few red cells, white cells and platelets. Myelodysplastic syndrome and myelofibrosis are marrow disorders that can also cause pancytopenia.

Hemolysis and blood loss raise the reticulocyte count. Anemia of chronic inflammation lowers it, since hepcidin traps iron and inflammatory cytokines blunt the marrow's response to erythropoietin, but it lowers the red cells only, not the white cells and platelets. Pure red cell aplasia also spares the white cells and platelets.
b3-w9-meds2024-q8-8.why: Reader report #148 is right: anemia of chronic inflammation is a hypoproliferative anemia with a low reticulocyte count. 04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia counts chronic disease among the causes whose reticulocytes are not raised. It is ruled out here because it does not cause pancytopenia, not because of the reticulocytes.
